segments.title: Review: Data structures, algorithms, graphs and traversals
segments.body:
A **data structure** stores data (a queue, a dictionary, a graph). An **algorithm** is a list of steps (BFS, sorting). A **graph** is vertices joined by edges. A **graph traversal** visits the vertices by following edges, and BFS is one.

Go back to module 1: the video “From a map to a graph” and “Key terms”.

segments.title: Review practice: data structures, algorithms, graphs and traversals
Review: Vertices, edges and direction
segments.body:
**Vertices** are the circles (the things). **Edges** are the lines (the connections), named by their two ends. If edges have **arrows**, the graph is **directed**; plain lines mean **undirected**. Two arrows between the same pair still make it directed.

Go back to module 1: “Worked example: reading a graph”, “Label the bus-stop graph”, the video “One-way or two-way?” and “Directed or undirected?”.

segments.title: Review practice: vertices, edges and direction
Review: Modelling a real situation as a graph
segments.body:
Ask three questions. What are the **things**? They're the vertices. What **connects** them? Those are the edges. Does each connection work **both ways**? If not, the graph is directed.

Go back to module 1: “Build the campus graph” and “Closing task: graphs in real life”.

segments.title: Review practice: modelling a real situation as a graph
Review: When BFS is the right tool
segments.body:
BFS is good for two jobs: finding the route with the **fewest edges**, and finding **everything reachable** from a start. It isn't for problems without connections, or where edges have different costs or lengths.

Go back to module 3: the video “Why BFS? The fewest walkways” and “When is BFS the right tool?”.

segments.title: Review practice: when BFS is the right tool
Review: Tracing BFS by hand
segments.body:
Each step: take the vertex at the **front** of the queue; it is now **visited**. Then add its neighbours that haven't been **found** yet to the **back**, in alphabetical order. A vertex is found as it joins the queue, so one that is still waiting is never added again. Repeat until the queue is empty.

Go back to module 3: the video “BFS step by step on the campus”, “Your turn: predict every step”, “Worked example: filling in a trace table” and “Your turn: a trace table”.

segments.title: Review practice: tracing BFS by hand
Objective 5 · fresh item: trace BFS from P, one row each time a vertex leaves the queue
Review: Writing BFS in Python
segments.body:
Before the loop: `visited = {start}`, `queue = deque([start])`, `order = []`. In the loop: `v = queue.popleft()`, `order.append(v)`, then for each `n` in `sorted(graph.adjacency[v])`, if it isn't in `visited` yet (the set of vertices found so far), add it to `visited` and `queue`. Return `order`.

Go back to module 4 (Build BFS).

segments.title: Review practice: writing BFS in python
Objective 6 · fresh item: fill in the missing parts of BFS
Review: Testing and debugging BFS
segments.body:
A good test builds a small graph, calls `bfs`, and asserts the **exact** list it should return. Two graphs catch most BFS bugs: one with a **cycle** (catches vertices visited twice) and one that's **disconnected** (catches vertices that shouldn't be reached).

Go back to module 5 (Test and debug).

activities.title: Review practice: data structures, algorithms, graphs and traversals

config.prompt: A to-do list app stores tasks in a queue and has a function that removes finished tasks one by one. Which is the data structure, and which is the algorithm?

options.label: The function is the data structure; the queue is the algorithm.
The queue is the data structure; removing tasks one by one is the algorithm.
They're both algorithms.

feedback.b: Not quite. That's the wrong way round. The queue stores the tasks; the function is the steps. Swap the roles.
feedback.c: Not quite. The queue stores data, so it's a data structure. Decide which one stores data.

hints.body: One part stores the tasks; one part does something.
Storing is a data structure's job.
Doing something step by step is an algorithm.
Answer: the queue is the data structure; the removing steps are the algorithm.

config.prompt: Which of these stores data, making it a data structure?

feedback.a: Not quite. That's an algorithm. Steps that do something are an algorithm. Find the option that stores information.
feedback.c: Not quite. That's a traversal. Visiting everything by following connections is a traversal. Find the option that stores information.

hints.body: A data structure stores data.
Sorting is something you do, so it's an algorithm.
Which option holds information?
Answer: the list of names.

config.prompt: Which of these is a list of steps, making it an algorithm?

options.label: A network of roads between the towns and cities in a province

A dictionary that maps each word to its meaning

feedback.a: Not quite. That's a data structure. A dictionary stores data; it doesn't do anything by itself. Find the option that is a set of steps.
feedback.b: Not quite. That's a graph. Roads between towns are a graph, which stores connections. Find the option that is a set of steps.

hints.body: An algorithm is a list of steps.
Dictionaries and road networks store data.
Which option describes doing something?
Answer: the steps for checking a word.

config.prompt: Match each term to an example of it.

right.label: Finding every friend-of-a-friend by following friend links

feedback.t1: Check “data structure”. A data structure stores data, like a queue of jobs. Find the example that stores things.

hints.body: One example stores things; one follows connections; one is neither.

config.prompt: What is a graph?

options.label: A set of vertices joined by edges
A chart with an x-axis and a y-axis
A list of steps for visiting every vertex and edge

feedback.b: Not quite. That's an algorithm. A graph is the thing being visited, not the steps. Think about vertices and edges.

Buildings were one part; walkways were the other.

feedback.c: Not quite. BFS doesn't store data. It's a list of steps. Decide which one does something.

hints.body: One stores items; one is a list of steps.
A queue stores items in order.

config.prompt: A graph has the edges A → B and B → A, and nothing else. Is it directed or undirected?

options.label: Undirected: you can go both ways between A and B.

feedback.b: Not quite. A graph can have any number of vertices. Look at whether the edges have arrows.

→ means an arrow.
Any arrow makes the graph directed, even if there's one each way.

activities.title: Review practice: when BFS is the right tool

config.prompt: Which problem is BFS a good fit for?

options.label: Finding the shortest route in kilometres, where roads have different lengths
Adding up the prices on a till slip
Finding the fewest bus changes between two stops

feedback.a: Not quite. BFS counts edges, not kilometres. Look for a problem about the fewest edges.
feedback.b: Not quite. There are no connections to follow. Look for a problem about the fewest edges.

hints.body: BFS counts edges.
Which problem is about the fewest connections?
Bus changes are edges between stops.
Answer: the fewest bus changes.

config.prompt: Find the fewest moves to solve a sliding-tile puzzle, where each position is a vertex and each move is an edge. Is BFS a good fit? Choose the answer with the right reason.

options.label: Yes. BFS checks every position one move away before any position two away.
No. BFS can't stop until it has visited every position, and there are too many.
Yes. BFS always takes the move that looks closest to the solved puzzle.

feedback.e: Not quite. BFS can stop the first time it reaches the solved position: every position one move away comes before any two moves away, so nothing it hasn't looked at yet can be closer. Ask: when has BFS found the fewest moves?
feedback.d: Not quite. BFS doesn't guess which move looks best: it takes positions in the order it found them, ring by ring. That is why the first time it reaches the solution, it has used the fewest moves. Ask: in what order does BFS take vertices?

hints.body: First ask: are there things joined by connections?
BFS is good at two jobs: the fewest edges, and reaching everything from a start.
Does this problem ask for one of those two jobs?
Answer: Yes. BFS checks every position one move away before any position two away.

config.prompt: Find the longest road trip between two towns without repeating a town. Is BFS a good fit? Choose the answer with the right reason.

options.label: No. BFS reaches each town by its shortest route, and this asks for the longest.
Yes. BFS visits every town once, and that is the longest trip there is.
Yes. The last ring BFS reaches is the furthest, so its route is the longest trip.

feedback.a: Not quite. Visiting every town isn't the same as finding one long route through them: BFS reaches each town by its shortest route. Ask: does BFS find the fewest edges or the most?
feedback.e: Not quite. The last ring is the furthest by the fewest edges, and BFS reaches it by its shortest route, not by the longest trip through the other towns. Ask: does BFS find the fewest edges or the most?

hints.body: First ask: are there things joined by connections?
BFS is good at two jobs: the fewest edges, and reaching everything from a start.
Does this problem ask for one of those two jobs?
Answer: No. BFS reaches each town by its shortest route, and this asks for the longest.

config.prompt: A clinic wants to find everyone who was in contact with a patient, and everyone in contact with one of those contacts. Is BFS a good fit? Choose the answer with the right reason.

options.label: No. BFS stops after the patient's direct contacts, so it never reaches their contacts.
Yes. BFS follows one chain of contacts to its end first.
Yes. BFS finds everyone one contact away, then two away, before going further.

feedback.h: Not quite. That is depth-first: following one chain to its end can reach someone three contacts away before a contact of a contact. BFS finishes each ring first. Ask: does BFS go wide or deep?
feedback.i: Not quite. BFS keeps going after the first ring: each contact who leaves the queue adds their own contacts to the back. Ask: what happens after the first ring?

hints.body: First ask: are there things joined by connections?
BFS is good at two jobs: the fewest edges, and reaching everything from a start.
Does this problem ask for one of those two jobs?
Answer: Yes. BFS finds everyone one contact away, then two away, before going further.

config.prompt: Sort a list of student numbers from smallest to largest. Is BFS a good fit? Choose the answer with the right reason.

options.label: Yes. BFS returns the vertices in order, so it sorts the student numbers.
No. Sorting a list has no edges to follow, so it isn't a traversal problem.
Yes. A queue keeps items in order, so BFS sorts them as they pass through it.

feedback.b: Not quite. BFS's order is the order it reaches vertices by following edges, not smallest to largest: on the campus it is A, C, E, B, F, D, G. Ask: are there edges to follow here?
feedback.e: Not quite. A queue keeps items in the order they arrived, first in, first out; it doesn't sort them. Ask: are there edges to follow here?

hints.body: First ask: are there things joined by connections?
BFS is good at two jobs: the fewest edges, and reaching everything from a start.
Does this problem ask for one of those two jobs?
Answer: No. Sorting a list has no edges to follow, so it isn't a traversal problem.

activities.title: Review practice: tracing BFS by hand

config.prompt: The queue is C, D. A and B have left the queue, and C and D are waiting in it. BFS processes C, whose neighbours are A, D and E. What is the queue now?

options.label: D, A, E
D, E
E, D

feedback.a: Not quite. A has already been found. A vertex that has been found never joins the queue again. Skip every neighbour that has been found.
feedback.c: Not quite. New vertices join at the back. D was already waiting, so it stays at the front. Remove C from the front, then add E at the back.

hints.body: C leaves from the front.
Check whether each neighbour has been found already. A vertex counts as found from the moment it joins the queue, even while it is still waiting.
Only E is new, and it joins at the back.
Answer: D, E.

activities.title: Objective 5 · fresh item: trace BFS from P, one row each time a vertex leaves the queue

hints.body: Each row starts by taking the vertex at the front of the previous queue.
Add the current vertex's neighbours that haven't been found yet to the back of the queue, in alphabetical order. A vertex is found when it joins the queue and visited when it leaves.
The first row: P leaves; the queue becomes S, U.
Answer: order P, S, U, Q, T, R. Queues after each row: [S, U]; [U, Q, T]; [Q, T, R]; [T, R]; [R]; [].

activities.title: Review practice: writing BFS in python

config.prompt: What belongs inside if n not in visited: in BFS?

options.label: visited.add(n) and queue.append(n)
order.append(n) and queue.append(n)
v = queue.popleft() and order.append(v)

feedback.d: Not quite. A vertex joins the order when it leaves the queue, not when it's found. What should happen to a newly found neighbour?
feedback.e: Not quite. Taking from the queue happens once per loop, before looking at neighbours. What should happen to a newly found neighbour?

hints.body: This runs for a neighbour that hasn't been found yet.
It needs to be remembered, and it needs to wait its turn.
Add it to the visited set, which holds every vertex found so far, and to the back of the queue.
Answer: visited.add(n) and queue.append(n).

activities.title: Objective 6 · fresh item: fill in the missing parts of BFS

1.[]: Not quite. deque([[]]) puts an empty list in the queue, not the start vertex, so BFS never starts from start. The queue starts with the start vertex.

2.visited: Not quite. visited already holds every vertex found, and a set has no append. Each vertex that leaves the queue joins the order list.

3.in: Not quite. With in, only vertices already found would be queued, so BFS never finds anything new. Queue a neighbour only if it is not in visited.

4.appendleft: Not quite. appendleft puts a new vertex at the front, so it is taken next and BFS goes deep instead of wide. BFS takes vertices from the front of the queue and adds new ones to the back. Check you use popleft() and append().

hints.body: The queue starts with the start vertex, and each vertex that leaves it joins the order.
A neighbour joins the queue only if it hasn't been found yet.
New vertices wait their turn at the back of the queue.
Answer: blank 1 is start, blank 2 is order, blank 3 is not in, and blank 4 is append.

activities.title: Review practice: testing and debugging BFS

config.prompt: Which test would catch a BFS that visits a vertex twice?

options.label: On a triangle A–B, B–C, C–A: assert bfs(g, "A") == ["A", "B", "C"]
On one vertex A with no edges at all: assert bfs(g, "A") == ["A"]
On a triangle A–B, B–C, C–A: assert len(bfs(g, "A")) > 0

feedback.b: Not quite. With no edges, nothing can be added twice, so the bug never shows. Use a graph with a cycle.
feedback.c: Not quite. That passes even if a vertex appears twice. Check the exact list. Assert the whole list.

hints.body: The bug only shows when a vertex can be found twice.
That needs a cycle.
Then check the exact result, not just its length.
Answer: the triangle test with the exact list.

activities.title: Objective 7 · fresh item 1 of 4: fix the faulty BFS

config.prompt: This BFS visits a vertex twice on a graph with a cycle. Replace the faulty line with a correction.

feedback.10: Not quite. order only holds vertices that have left the queue, not ones still waiting, so a waiting vertex can be added again. Check against the vertices found so far instead.

hints.body: Run it on a graph with a cycle. What goes wrong?
Look at the condition before a neighbour joins the queue.
order only holds vertices that have left the queue, not ones still waiting.
Answer: change if n not in order: to if n not in visited:.

activities.title: Objective 7 · fresh item 2 of 4: fix the faulty BFS

config.prompt: This BFS visits the start vertex twice on most graphs. Replace the faulty line with a correction.

feedback.3: Not quite. The start vertex is in the queue but never added to visited, the set of vertices found so far, so a neighbour can add it again. Start with the start vertex already in visited.

hints.body: Run it on a graph with a cycle through the start. What goes wrong?
Look at what's in visited before the loop.
The start vertex is in the queue but never added to visited, so a neighbour can add it again.
Answer: change visited = set() to visited = {start}.

activities.title: Objective 7 · fresh item 3 of 4: choose the tests that catch the bug

config.prompt: This BFS has a bug. Choose every test case it fails: each one is a graph, a start vertex and the order a correct BFS visits it in.

feedback.cycle: A's neighbours lead back to A, which was never added to visited, so the faulty version visits A twice and fails it.
feedback.residence: P's neighbours lead back to P, which was never added to visited, so the faulty version visits P twice and fails it.
feedback.out-of-order: A's neighbours lead back to A, which was never added to visited, so the faulty version visits A twice and fails it.
feedback.two-islands: B leads back to A, which was never added to visited, so the faulty version visits A twice and fails it.

activities.title: Objective 7 · fresh item 4 of 4: choose the tests that catch the bug

config.prompt: This BFS has a bug. Choose every test case it fails: each one is a graph, a start vertex and the order a correct BFS visits it in.

feedback.cycle: A's neighbours B, C and D all join the queue. The faulty version takes D, the newest, next instead of B, so it fails this test.
feedback.residence: P's neighbours Q and R both join the queue. The faulty version takes R, the newest, before Q, so it fails this test.
feedback.out-of-order: A's neighbours B, C and E all join the queue. The faulty version takes E, the newest, first, so it fails this test.
feedback.two-islands: No vertex here ever has two vertices waiting in the queue at once, so newest and oldest are the same: the faulty version passes it.
feedback.one-way: Each vertex here finds at most one new vertex, so the queue never holds two at once: the faulty version passes it.
feedback.one-vertex: There is only A, so there is nothing to take in the wrong order: the faulty version passes it.

hints.body: Read the line that takes a vertex out of the queue.
pop() takes the vertex that joined last, from the back, so the search goes deep instead of wide.
That only changes the order when two or more vertices are waiting in the queue at the same time.
Answer: cycle, residence and out-of-order. The faulty version passes the other three.
